Storm Damage Disrupts Guernsey Technology Services Sites

A severe Atlantic storm has inflicted significant damage on Technology Services industry premises across Guernsey, leaving several firms struggling to maintain operations as heavy winds and flooding continue to impact the island. The storm, which made landfall late Tuesday night, has brought record rainfall and gusts exceeding 80 mph, causing widespread disruption to company offices, data centers, and other critical facilities in the sector.

According to the Guernsey Technology Services Association, more than a dozen industry sites have reported water ingress, roof damage, or flooding of ground floors. The majority of affected sites are concentrated in St. Peter Port and the southern parishes, where localized flooding has been most severe. “We are seeing unprecedented damage to our members’ premises,” said Association Chairperson Helen Roussel. “Several data centers have had to initiate emergency protocols to protect core infrastructure, and some office buildings remain inaccessible due to floodwaters.”

The ongoing weather event has forced many firms to enact contingency plans, including the temporary relocation of critical staff and the shutdown of non-essential operations. “Our main priority is the safety of our workforce,” said a spokesperson for ChannelTech Solutions, one of the island’s largest providers of software and managed IT services. “We have asked staff based in the affected offices to work remotely where possible, but the situation remains volatile as the storm continues.”

Industry analysts estimate that up to 40% of local Technology Services industry capacity is currently affected, with some sites expected to remain offline for several days. “The biggest challenge for the sector is the physical damage to server rooms and the disruption of access for employees,” noted Michael Le Page, an independent industry consultant. “Many firms have invested in disaster recovery plans, but the scale and duration of this event are testing those preparations.”

Unions representing Technology Services workers have expressed concern about both safety and the potential for longer-term operational impacts. “We are in close contact with employers to ensure all necessary measures are taken to protect staff and minimize risks,” said Marie Lenfestey of the Guernsey Tech Workers’ Union.

The Guernsey Technology Services Association has called for urgent coordination among its members to address immediate needs and begin planning for recovery once the storm abates. With meteorologists forecasting further heavy rain and high winds, the full extent of the damage remains unclear.
